hooks.text: A subatomic particle hit Earth with the energy of a fast-pitched baseball.
One single proton carried 47 million times the energy of our best colliders.
The fastest visitor to Earth was invisible and hit like a professional athlete.

title: The Invisible Particle That Hits Like a Baseball
description: In 1991, the Oh-My-God particle struck Earth's atmosphere with more energy than any human-built machine could ever produce.

beats.text: A subatomic particle hit Earth with the energy of a fast-pitched baseball.
beats.visual: artist's concept of a high-energy cosmic ray entering Earth's atmosphere

beats.text: In October 1991, the Fly's Eye detector in Utah captured a visitor traveling at nearly light speed.
beats.visual: the Fly's Eye detector array in Dugway, Utah

beats.text: Dubbed the Oh-My-God particle, this single proton packed 320 exaelectronvolts of energy.
beats.visual: diagram of an extensive air shower hitting the atmosphere

beats.text: That is forty-seven million times more energy than our most powerful human-built accelerators.
beats.visual: the Large Hadron Collider tunnel at CERN

beats.text: Most people assume such force must come from a massive, visible cosmic engine.
beats.visual: an active galactic nucleus with powerful jets powered by a black hole

beats.text: But tracing its path back reveals absolutely nothing in the darkness where it began.
beats.visual: the Cosmic Microwave Background radiation map

beats.text: In 2021, the Amaterasu particle arrived with similar power from a completely empty cosmic void.
beats.visual: the Telescope Array Project in the Utah desert

beats.text: These invisible missiles prove the universe can hit us with the energy of a fast-pitched baseball.
beats.visual: artist's concept of a cosmic ray shower over the Utah desert

better_than_last: This script corrects beat claims to strictly map to the research source claims while maintaining the myth-versus-fact structure and seamless looping.
